label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **Brent crude settled at $116.72, its highest since April 29**, on reports that the U.S. and Israel plan new Iran strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms (CNBC, Fox News). Trump told a Florida rally the U.S. may do 'another little epic fury' unless Iran agrees to a deal, which sits oddly beside his Oct. 8 no-strike pledge (Fox News, The Hill). Stocks fell, with the Dow down 1.23 percent to 52,215.16 and the S&P 500 off 0.52 percent (CNBC). American Express said it will cut about 5 percent of its workforce to prepare for AI (CNBC, Bloomberg). In California, the Justice Department's bid to block 20,000 ballots heads to a hearing before Judge David Carter next week, after DOJ asked the Ninth Circuit to step in (The Hill, NBC News). Polls from Fox News, CNN and NPR keep **Democrats ahead by about 10 points** with 11 days to go (Fox News, CNN, NPR). Closer to home, **Bay Area transit tax RTM is on the Nov. 3 ballot**, and agencies say a defeat would bring deep cuts (KQED, SF Chronicle). NASA briefed on its Artemis plan, with a crewed Earth-orbit test in 2027 and a landing targeted for 2028 (NASA, Space.com). Microsoft and Nvidia are building **agent security outside the AI model** (TechCrunch). Merck and Moderna's mRNA melanoma vaccine **cut recurrence risk 42 percent**, with full data due Saturday (CNN).

alerts.text: Brent settled at $116.72, so expect gas prices to keep climbing if Iran strike fears hold.
Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 and Amazon Oct. 29 after the close; Apple follows Nov. 2.
Judge Carter hears DOJ's bid to block 20,000 California ballots next week, and the Ninth Circuit could act sooner.
Caltrans closes westbound I-80 in San Francisco through Oct. 26, which may push traffic onto transit (KQED).

highlights.text: Brent hits $116.72, the highest settlement since April, on reported post-midterm Iran strike plans.
Trump says the U.S. may strike Iran again, despite his pledge to wait until after the midterms.
DOJ's push to block 20,000 California ballots heads to a hearing before Judge Carter next week.
Dow falls 1.2 percent as oil climbs and AI spending worries linger.
Microsoft and Nvidia put AI agent security outside the model.

markets.wrap: The Dow fell 1.23 percent to 52,215.16, the S&P 500 lost 0.52 percent and the Nasdaq slipped 0.21 percent as **oil climbed on Iran strike fears** (CNBC). Brent settled at $116.72, its highest since April 29, and American Express fell more than 3 percent on a 5 percent workforce cut (CNBC). The 10-year yield ended near 5 percent after Thursday's biggest one-day drop since March 2023, driven by **AI spending worries** (CNBC). Microsoft was the only watchlist gainer; no watchlist stock moved more than 2 percent.

stories.title: Polls show Democrats ahead for the Nov. 3 midterms
stories.summary: Fox, CNN and NPR polls all put Democrats ahead on the House ballot and Trump's approval near record lows.
story: A Fox News poll taken Oct. 9-12 puts Trump's approval at 36 percent, the lowest in any Fox survey of his two terms, and shows Democrats ahead 54 to 45 on the House ballot (Fox News). Approval among Republicans fell to 76 percent in that poll. The Washington Examiner also reported a new low for Trump's approval despite his campaign push.

Other pollsters see the same shape. A CNN/SSRS poll from Oct. 15-18 has Democrats up 49 to 39 on the congressional ballot, the widest margin in that poll since just before the 2020 election, with Trump at 32 percent approval (CNN). NPR's poll of Oct. 13-19 found likely voters preferring a Democrat 54 to 42 and Trump at 34 percent approval, 62 percent disapproval (NPR). The Hill summarized the trend as a 10-point Democratic edge.

The Senate is tighter. CNN's poll averages show Maine at 49 to 48 for Democrat Troy Jackson over Susan Collins, Ohio at 49 to 44 for Sherrod Brown over Jon Husted, and Michigan at 49 to 47 for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed over Mike Rogers. An Emerson poll has Texas at 48 to 46 for Democrat James Talarico over Ken Paxton, inside the margin of error (The Hill).

Republicans say the polls can be beaten. Fox's Republican co-pollster Daron Shaw said the party still has time to close gaps, though it is getting late, and conservative commentators argue that the Democratic Party's leftward drift gives the GOP an opening with moderates (Fox News).
facts: Fox News poll, Oct. 9-12: Trump approval 36%, a record low in Fox polling.
Same poll: Democrats lead the House ballot 54% to 45%.
CNN/SSRS, Oct. 15-18: Democrats 49%, Republicans 39%; Trump approval 32%.
NPR poll, Oct. 13-19: likely voters prefer a Democrat 54% to 42%.
Election Day is Nov. 3.
stories.next: Early voting is under way; watch fresh NYT/Siena and Emerson polls before Nov. 3.
stories.left: Voters are telling every pollster the same thing: costs are too high and they want a check on the president. With Trump below 40 percent in every major survey, Democrats argue the House is theirs to win and the Senate is in play. They say the fight over election rules shows an administration worried about the result.
stories.right: Polls are snapshots, and conservatives note that midterm electorates differ from poll samples. Republicans say Democratic primary wins by left-wing candidates let them paint the whole party as extreme, and they point to strong fundraising and Speaker Johnson's confidence that the majority holds. A late swing among low-propensity voters could narrow the gap.

stories.title: Justice Department asks courts to block counting of 20,000 California ballots; hearing set for next week
stories.summary: DOJ says all 20,000 people it flagged are noncitizens; California says its own sample shows many were never mailed ballots.
story: The Justice Department sued California on Oct. 15 in Los Angeles federal court, asking the court to bar officials from counting mail ballots tied to about 20,000 registrants it calls likely noncitizens, or to force the state to verify their citizenship first (Fox News, SF Chronicle). Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in the Central District, said investigators reviewed every name and concluded all 20,000 are noncitizens who likely received ballots (Fox News).

California disputes the list. Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote that the administration listed people it "believes" are "likely" noncitizens, and a Los Angeles County official said that in a 200-record sample, 112 matched canceled or inactive registrations that were not mailed ballots (SF Chronicle, CalMatters). The county also said it lacks the data to verify citizenship.

Judge David Carter scheduled a hearing next week on the emergency request, and DOJ then asked the Ninth Circuit to step in before he ruled, calling the delay a 'constructive denial' (The Hill, NBC News). Prosecutors separately charged 28 green-card holders from the list with illegal voting (CalMatters). Newsom called the suit an attempt to make California 'violate federal law' (Fox News).

Separately, on Oct. 21 U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín restricted DHS field operations aimed at finding noncitizen voters in nine states, including California, finding they likely violate the Voting Rights Act because the target list was 'voluminous and unreliable' (NPR). She delayed enforcement until Friday to let the government appeal. DHS says it is 'laser focused' on aliens who vote (NPR). I found no ruling yet from Carter or the Ninth Circuit.
facts: DOJ filed suit Oct. 15 in Los Angeles federal court.
The list has about 20,000 registrants DOJ calls likely noncitizens.
LA County's sample found 112 of 200 records tied to canceled or inactive registrations.
Judge Carter set a hearing for next week; DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit.
A separate judge limited DHS noncitizen-voter field operations in nine states.
stories.next: Watch for Judge Carter's hearing next week and any Ninth Circuit order; the exact date was not reported.
stories.left: Democrats and California officials say the list is unreliable and that sweeping the ballots of tens of thousands of registrants, some never mailed a ballot, risks disenfranchising citizens days before an election. They call threats of criminal charges against election workers intimidation and note that courts have repeatedly rejected the DOJ's voter-roll demands.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that counting ballots from noncitizens would dilute citizens' votes, and that the 28 criminal charges show the problem is real. They say federal agencies hold the immigration records counties lack, and that a state refusing to cooperate with a federal check invites distrust in the result.
stories.flag: Essayli's claim that every name is a verified noncitizen has not been independently confirmed; California disputes it.

stories.title: Trump says the U.S. could hit Iran again, two weeks after pledging to wait until after the midterms
stories.summary: At a Florida rally Trump said the U.S. may do 'another little epic fury' unless Iran agrees to a deal, raising questions about his Oct. 8 pledge.
story: Speaking Friday in Fort Myers, Florida, at a rally for Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds, President Trump said the United States could strike Iran again if Tehran does not reach a deal. 'We may do another little epic fury, or they'll agree,' he said, according to Fox News and The Hill's coverage of the event. He also said the U.S. could take Iran's oil, and called the Strait of Hormuz 'totally ours' (Fox News, NBC News).

The remarks sit awkwardly beside his Oct. 8 post on Truth Social saying the U.S. 'will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections' on Nov. 3 (The Hill, CNN). A White House deputy press secretary repeated that line, while other officials have said Trump keeps 'all options' open. The New York Times has reported that the U.S. and Israel are drafting plans to resume strikes after Nov. 3 (CNBC).

The politics are hard for Republicans. The Washington Examiner interviewed rally attendees who backed Trump's policies but worried about high gas prices, and Fox News reported that GOP strategists see the clock ticking as Iran keeps pressure on fuel costs. Senate Majority Leader John Thune earlier said the war had 'sort of trumped everything else' in the campaign (Washington Examiner).
I could not confirm how the White House squares the rally comments with the pledge. A strike before Nov. 3 would break the promise, and a strike after it would fit the reported plans.
stories.flag: Whether the rally remarks signal a change from the Oct. 8 no-strike pledge is not confirmed; the White House had not clarified in the coverage I found.
facts: Trump spoke Friday, Oct. 23, in Fort Myers, Florida, for Byron Donalds.
He said the U.S. 'may do another little epic fury, or they'll agree.'
On Oct. 8 he wrote that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms.
The New York Times reported U.S. and Israeli plans to resume strikes after Nov. 3.
Rally attendees told the Washington Examiner they worry about gas prices.
stories.left: Democrats argue that a president who promises restraint for the election and talks of 'epic fury' days later is treating a war as a campaign tool. They say Congress has not authorized an open-ended conflict, that gas prices are the price ordinary families already pay, and that threats to 'take the whole country' make a deal harder.
stories.right: Republicans say credible force is how Iran is kept from a nuclear weapon. Secretary of State Rubio has argued that 'the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations.' Supporters say Trump is keeping Tehran guessing and that the pledge covered the weeks before the vote, not the whole war.
stories.next: Watch for any strike or White House clarification before Nov. 3, and for Israel's Oct. 27 election.

stories.title: Bay Area voters decide a $14 billion transit sales tax on Nov. 3
stories.summary: Regional Measure RTM would add a sales tax in five counties, including Alameda County, while agencies publish cuts they say would follow a defeat.
story: Bay Area voters will decide Regional Measure RTM on Nov. 3. It would add a 14-year sales tax of 0.5 percent in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and 1 percent in San Francisco, raising about $980 million a year by Metropolitan Transportation Commission figures (KQED, SF Chronicle). Fremont is in Alameda County, so its voters are in the half-cent zone. San Francisco has a separate Muni parcel tax, Proposition H.

Because citizens put it on the ballot, it needs a simple majority, not two-thirds (SF Chronicle). Agencies have published contingency plans. BART has said it could close up to 15 stations and run trains every half hour, and Caltrain has warned of ending weekend service, closing a large share of stations and moving to hourly weekday trains (SF Chronicle). Muni says it would cut about 20 routes if either measure fails. Station counts have changed over the campaign, and KQED reports Caltrain naming 10 stations.

Opponents, led by the Committee for Affordable Bay Area Transit, say agencies should spend existing money first. They point to more than $6 billion in taxes, tolls and grants the agencies received in fiscal 2024-25 and propose pausing capital projects such as BART Silicon Valley Phase II (KQED). Spokesperson Marc Joffe has said, 'We don't agree that the failure of RTM would necessitate slashing service.' Supporters at Connect Bay Area say most capital money cannot legally pay for operations.
A judge in Santa Clara County ruled in August that opponents failed to show the ballot question was biased (KQED). The SF Chronicle editorial board endorses the measure.
stories.flag: Agency cut lists differ by date and source; the station counts above are the latest I found and may change.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found comes from KQED and the SF Chronicle; I found no right-leaning outlet reporting on the measure.
facts: RTM is on the Nov. 3 ballot in five Bay Area counties.
The tax is 0.5% in Alameda County and 1% in San Francisco, for 14 years.
It would raise about $980 million a year (MTC figures).
It needs a simple majority.
Opponents say agencies should use existing funds first.
stories.left: Supporters argue transit is basic infrastructure and that a broad sales tax is the fastest way to prevent a service spiral that would push more cars onto the Bay Bridge. They cite a report that Bay Bridge delays could double if the measures fail, and say cuts would fall hardest on riders without cars.
stories.right: Critics call a sales tax regressive and say agencies have not exhausted savings, overtime or capital funds. Former state Sen. Steve Glazer has described it as a regressive tax on the region's poorest residents. They argue that voters should demand reform and a slimmer measure before approving $14 billion.
stories.next: Election Day is Nov. 3. If the measure fails, the AC Transit board expects to consider a final service-cut plan on Dec. 9.

stories.title: California state workers stage first-ever one-day strike
stories.summary: About 100,000 SEIU Local 1000 members fought over pay, health costs and Newsom's office mandate; mediation resumes Oct. 30.
story: Thousands of California state workers walked off the job on Oct. 21 in a one-day strike by SEIU Local 1000, the first in the union's history, over pay, health care costs and remote-work rules (CalMatters, AP). The union represents about 100,000 state employees, and its contract expired June 30. Some DMV, parks and other services were limited (CalMatters).

Members voted 96.2 percent to authorize the strike. The union says the state is bargaining in bad faith, and the state labor board sided with it, finding that CalHR refused to meet and confer in good faith (CalMatters). The state's human resources department says it "remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement."

Both sides are due back in mediation Oct. 30, and the union has said it could escalate if talks stall (CalMatters). The dispute lands in Gov. Newsom's final months in office and centers on his four-day in-office requirement and state health contributions.
Newsom earlier vetoed a bill that would have given striking workers unemployment benefits (Fox Business).
facts: The strike took place Oct. 21 and lasted one day.
SEIU Local 1000 represents about 100,000 state workers.
96.2% of voting members authorized the strike.
The labor board found CalHR refused to meet and confer in good faith.
Mediation resumes Oct. 30.
stories.next: Mediation between SEIU Local 1000 and the state resumes Oct. 30.
stories.left: The union argues that workers who kept California running through the pandemic deserve a raise, affordable health care and flexibility, and that the state broke labor law by refusing to bargain. Supporters say a rested, fairly paid workforce serves the public better than a four-day office mandate.
stories.right: Critics say public-employee strikes hurt residents who need the DMV and parks, and they point to a state budget under strain. They argue return-to-office rules are a reasonable management call and that Newsom's veto of strike benefits reflects limits on what taxpayers can fund.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning coverage of this strike found beyond Fox Business's report on Newsom's earlier veto.

stories.title: Brent hits its highest settlement since April as U.S. and Israel reportedly plan post-midterm Iran strikes
stories.summary: Brent settled at $116.72 as Houthi attacks on Saudi sites and reports of U.S.-Israeli strike plans fed supply fears; Netanyahu urged toppling Iran's regime.
story: Brent crude settled at $116.72 a barrel on Friday, up 3.1 percent and the highest settlement since April 29, while U.S. crude rose 3.8 percent as traders priced in a possible return of U.S. strikes on Iran (CNBC). Brent has gained for three straight weeks, up 6.2 percent this week. The trigger is a New York Times report that the U.S. and Israel are drafting plans to resume strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms, with targets including energy infrastructure, nuclear sites and missile and drone arsenals (Fox News, CNBC).

Supply worries added to the move. Iran-backed Houthi militants attacked Saudi oil installations, and Reuters reported that Saudi Aramco told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely (CNBC). CNBC also reported that the U.S. pulled diplomats from Saudi Arabia. Iran issued what Fox News called a 'serious warning' to U.S. forces in the region.

Politics is pushing in both directions. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday night that the U.S. and Israel must overthrow Iran's regime, and Trump has endorsed him ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 election (Fox News). Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says the U.S. must lift sanctions and end threats before talks (Fox News). Trump says the U.S. is not negotiating (CNBC).
Higher crude is already reaching businesses. American Airlines said it expects a bigger 2026 loss because of the jet fuel spike (CNBC).
stories.flag: The strike plans come from a New York Times report relayed by other outlets and are not confirmed by officials; Trump has pledged no attack before Nov. 3.
facts: Brent settled at $116.72, up 3.1%, the highest settlement since April 29 (CNBC).
U.S. crude rose 3.8% on the day.
Aramco told staff at its Dhahran headquarters to evacuate, per Reuters.
Netanyahu called for overthrowing Iran's regime; Israel votes Oct. 27.
Iran says the U.S. must lift sanctions before talks.
stories.left: Critics say a war without clear goals or congressional approval is now costing American families at the pump, and that Netanyahu's call for regime change shows why open-ended escalation is dangerous. They want Washington to press for talks and not let an Israeli election set U.S. timing.
stories.right: Supporters say Iran's regime is the root of the threat to Gulf shipping and to Israel, and that Houthi and Iranian attacks on Saudi sites show deterrence has not yet worked. They argue that a short, hard strike on energy and nuclear targets is better than a long standoff, and that Iran's demands show it is not bargaining in good faith.
stories.next: Watch Monday's oil open, any Hormuz or Saudi attack, and Israel's Oct. 27 election.

stories.title: Putin agrees in principle to resume three-way Ukraine talks after Nov. 10
stories.summary: Witkoff met Putin Oct. 21 and Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard; Kyiv was struck hours later.
story: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, and Putin agreed in principle to restart three-way talks with Kyiv and Washington after Nov. 10, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said (The Hill). The Kremlin said Abu Dhabi could host the next round, with no date set. Russia also freed American Stephen Hubbard (NBC News).

Hours after the announcement, Russia hit Kyiv with a large missile and drone attack that killed two people and injured 34, Zelensky said (CNN, The Hill). Zelensky wants a meeting by early November and says Moscow has repeatedly promised talks and then canceled.

Zelensky told CNN there is "nothing personal" between him and Trump, though the relationship has soured over a U.S. diesel deal with Russia and sanctions waivers (CNN). Czech President Petr Pavel said the diesel deal derailed progress (The Hill). Zelensky says Ukraine would accept a freeze on the current front line but not give up territory it holds.
Trump says his team is "the closest we've been" to a settlement; the Kremlin said earlier proposals contained little of value.
facts: Witkoff met Putin Oct. 21 in St. Petersburg.
Putin agreed in principle to talks after Nov. 10; Abu Dhabi is a possible venue.
Russia's attack on Kyiv killed two and injured 34.
Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard.
Zelensky would accept a freeze on the front line.
stories.next: No date is set; watch for a Nov. 10-plus meeting announcement.
stories.left: Critics say easing sanctions on Russian diesel rewarded Putin while he kept bombing Kyiv, and that the talks are a stalling tactic. They want more aid to Ukraine and tougher sanctions before any deal that rewards aggression.
stories.right: Supporters argue that only direct engagement with Moscow can end the war, that Europe should carry more of the burden, and that Kyiv must face the reality of the front line. They credit the push for the Hubbard release as a sign diplomacy can work.
stories.blindspot: Little right-leaning coverage of this round turned up in my searches.

stories.title: American Express cuts about 5 percent of its workforce to prepare for AI
stories.summary: Amex announced about 3,500 job cuts with earnings and raised its 2026 guidance; shares fell more than 3 percent.
story: American Express said Friday it will cut about 5 percent of its global workforce alongside third-quarter results, taking a $336 million restructuring charge (CNBC). CEO Stephen Squeri told Bloomberg TV the company has 78,000 employees, which puts the cut near 3,500 jobs. Shares fell more than 3 percent, and Amex was a drag on the Dow (CNBC).

CFO Christophe Le Caillec said the company is reducing layers and widening spans of control so it can automate and use AI in the coming quarters and years (CNBC). Bloomberg reported that Amex raised its 2026 earnings guidance after beating Wall Street estimates, and framed the cuts as a way for Squeri to hold down rising costs.

The announcement fits a pattern in financial services, where banks and card companies are trying to replace repetitive roles with automation. It also lands in a week when investors are asking whether AI spending will pay off, so the same technology is both a cost for tech companies and a reason for cuts elsewhere.
stories.blindspot: I found coverage only from CNBC and Bloomberg; no left- or right-leaning outlet reporting on this was returned.
facts: Amex will cut about 5% of its global workforce.
The company has 78,000 employees, so roughly 3,500 jobs are affected.
The restructuring charge is $336 million.
Amex raised its 2026 earnings guidance (Bloomberg).
Shares fell more than 3% on Friday.
stories.left: Labor advocates argue that a profitable company cutting thousands of jobs in the name of AI shifts gains to shareholders while workers carry the risk. They call for notice rules, severance and retraining paid for by firms that automate.
stories.right: Free-market voices say companies must adapt to stay competitive and that automation has historically created new jobs. They oppose mandates on layoffs, arguing they would slow hiring, and favor skills training and a strong economy that absorbs displaced workers.
stories.next: Watch whether other card issuers and banks announce AI-linked cuts in their earnings next week.

stories.title: Dow drops 1.2 percent as oil climbs and AI spending worries linger
stories.summary: The Dow lost 652.82 points, the S&P 500 fell 0.52 percent and the Nasdaq slipped 0.21 percent on a risk-off Friday.
story: Stocks ended the week lower on Friday as oil rose and AI spending worries lingered. The Dow fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to 52,215.16. The S&P 500 slipped 0.52 percent to 7,623.68, and the Nasdaq lost 0.21 percent to 25,955.34 (CNBC). For the week the S&P 500 lost 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq 0.7 percent, while the Dow gained 0.4 percent.

Oil drove the tone. Brent settled at $116.72 and U.S. crude at $103.27 on reports of planned Iran strikes (CNBC). American Express fell more than 3 percent after announcing job cuts (CNBC). On Thursday the Nasdaq had dropped 2.6 percent, its worst day since June, on AI funding fears.

Bonds were also in play. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 17 basis points to 4.972 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop since March 2023, as investors sought safety from AI worries, then rose back to about 5 percent Friday as oil lifted inflation fears (CNBC). Among your watchlist, only Microsoft rose, up 0.66 percent, and Alphabet fell 1.24 percent.

Next week brings Big Tech earnings. Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 and Amazon Oct. 29, all after the close, and Apple follows Nov. 2. CNBC says the Fed meets next week and is not expected to change rates.
facts: Weekly: S&P 500 -0.5%, Nasdaq -0.7%, Dow +0.4% (CNBC).
Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28; Amazon Oct. 29.
stories.why: Oil above $100 and doubts about AI financing are the two forces moving stocks, and next week's capex guidance from Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon will test the second one.
stories.next: Alphabet and Microsoft earnings on Oct. 28 after the close, then Amazon on Oct. 29.

stories.title: IBM's Anderon builds a 300 mm quantum chip foundry with $1 billion in CHIPS money
stories.summary: Commerce finalized an award of up to $1 billion, matched by IBM, for a quantum wafer foundry in Albany.
story: The Commerce Department finalized a CHIPS and Science Act R&D award of up to $1 billion for Anderon, a quantum foundry IBM set up this year, and IBM is matching it with $1 billion in cash plus intellectual property and staff (IEEE Spectrum). Anderon is based in Albany, New York, and will run a 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry.

It builds on work at Albany NanoTech, where IBM has made quantum wafers for more than five years. CEO Mukesh Khare said first wafers are already moving through a production-scale line (IEEE Spectrum).
The award was first reported in May as part of a $2 billion package for nine quantum companies in which the government takes minority equity stakes (CNBC, Bloomberg).
The pitch is a fabless model for quantum chips: other companies design qubit devices and a dedicated fab builds them, as classical chip foundries do.
facts: Award: up to $1 billion from CHIPS and Science Act funds.
IBM is matching with $1 billion in cash.
The fab uses 300 mm wafers in Albany, New York.
The government takes a minority equity stake (CNBC).
stories.next: Watch for the first outside design customers for Anderon wafers.
stories.why: Quantum chips are mostly built in small labs. A shared, standard fab could cut costs and speed up designs the way foundries did for classical chips.
stories.flag: Sources disagree on the exact date of the final award; IEEE Spectrum dates it Sept. 16.

stories.title: Applied Materials opens $5 billion EPIC Center in Sunnyvale
stories.summary: The facility puts TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix in one building with equipment makers and universities.
story: Applied Materials opened its EPIC Center in Sunnyvale on Oct. 12, calling it the world's largest facility for collaborative semiconductor process and equipment R&D, with $5 billion in planned investment as customer projects start (Applied Materials, Evertiq). It has nearly four acres of cleanroom space.

Founding partners are TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix. Broadcom, Advantest, SCREEN, KIOXIA and Besi are innovation partners, and Arizona State, RPI, Stanford, UC Berkeley and UCLA are research partners (Applied Materials).
CEO Gary Dickerson framed it as part of the race for AI leadership, and Applied says working side by side could cut years off the path from concept to commercial production.
IEEE Spectrum has tied it to a wave of AI-driven semiconductor R&D spending.
facts: Opened Oct. 12 in Sunnyvale, California.
Planned investment: $5 billion over time.
Founding partners: TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix.
About four acres of cleanroom space.
stories.next: Watch for the first announced joint projects from the partners.
stories.why: Putting chipmakers and toolmakers together early is meant to shorten the time to new chip processes, and it keeps this work in the Bay Area.

stories.title: NASA updates its Artemis plan: Earth-orbit test in 2027, first landing targeted for 2028
stories.summary: NASA leaders briefed at Kennedy on Artemis III and on speeding up Artemis IV, the first planned landing.
story: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya and Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons gave an update Friday at Kennedy Space Center on returning astronauts to the Moon's surface in 2028. NASA says the briefing covered Artemis III, a 2027 mission that would send four astronauts to low Earth orbit, and efforts to speed up Artemis IV, the first planned landing (NASA).

The plan dates to February, when Isaacman turned Artemis III from a lunar landing into an Earth-orbit test in which Orion docks with one or more commercial landers, and moved the first landing to Artemis IV in 2028 (Space.com). The Artemis III crew named in June is Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas and ESA's Luca Parmitano (ADN).

The lander schedules are the risk. Space.com reports SpaceX plans an uncrewed lunar landing test in the fourth quarter of 2027, and Blue Origin's New Glenn is still grounded after a May pad explosion, with a Reuters report suggesting a return to flight in early 2027. NASA's inspector general said earlier this year it was too early to judge whether speeding up either lander is feasible.
stories.flag: I could only find NASA's summary of the briefing, not a full account, so any new dates, budgets or hardware changes announced there are not included.
facts: The briefing was Oct. 23 at Kennedy Space Center.
Artemis III is a 2027 low-Earth-orbit mission with four astronauts.
Artemis IV is planned as the first landing, in 2028.
SpaceX targets an uncrewed landing test in Q4 2027 (Space.com).
New Glenn has been grounded since a May pad explosion.
stories.why: A 2028 landing depends on two commercial landers and new suits all working on schedule, and the 2027 docking test is the first real check.
stories.next: Watch for NASA's detailed schedule and for Blue Origin's New Glenn return to flight.

stories.title: NASA's Roman telescope enters final commissioning
stories.summary: Engineers say the observatory and its primary instrument are working; first images are expected in early 2027.
story: NASA says its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has entered its final commissioning phase after a checkout of the observatory and its primary instrument, and engineers say it is fully functional (NASA). Roman launched on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy on Aug. 30 (Space.com, Astronomy).

After commissioning and calibration, first images are expected in early 2027 (Space.com). The wide-field instrument's image quality and the coronagraph's light-blocking performance have not yet been verified in space.
Roman is built to survey large areas of sky for dark energy, exoplanets and distant galaxies.
facts: Launched Aug. 30 on a Falcon Heavy.
NASA reports the observatory and primary instrument are fully functional.
First images are expected in early 2027.
Wide-field imaging and coronagraph performance are not yet verified in space.
stories.next: Watch for first-light images in early 2027.
stories.why: Roman's wide view lets it map far more sky than Hubble, which matters for dark energy and exoplanet surveys.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet, an always-on agent app
stories.summary: The research-preview app watches connected apps and sends a daily brief, built on Claude Opus 5.5.
story: Anthropic announced Claude Duet on Oct. 21, a standalone agent app for professionals and small-business owners that monitors connected apps and flags items needing attention instead of waiting for prompts (Reuters via KFGO, TechCrunch). It sends a morning brief and messages users only when something needs attention.

It runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and uses the connectors in the Claude Marketplace, which Reuters puts at more than 6,000 (Reuters via KFGO). Users can hand it tasks by text or voice in one thread, from scheduling to building dashboards or prototypes.

It is a waitlisted research preview on iOS, Android and claude.ai for U.S. Pro and Max subscribers. Anthropic acknowledges it can misjudge urgency and asks for approval before sensitive actions (Reuters via KFGO).
Coverage frames it as a response to OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse and similar always-on agents (iPhone in Canada).
facts: Announced Oct. 21; research preview.
Built on Claude Opus 5.5.
Available to U.S. Pro and Max subscribers by waitlist.
Asks for approval before sensitive actions.
stories.next: Watch the waitlist rollout and how it handles urgency calls in early use.
stories.why: Moving from chat to always-on agents shifts AI from tool to assistant. The hard parts are trust, permissions and false alarms.
stories.flag: Reports differ on whether the announcement was Wednesday or Thursday.

stories.title: Microsoft and Nvidia move AI agent security outside the model
stories.summary: Microsoft's Guardian Agents and Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform both put monitoring and limits outside the AI model.
story: Microsoft and Nvidia are both building security that sits outside the AI model. TechCrunch reported on Oct. 19 that Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature monitors the AI agents a company uses, as part of Project Perception, introduced in June. CEO Satya Nadella has argued that enterprises should stop relying on model providers' safety claims and run separate monitoring that the labs do not control, treating agents like potential insider threats (TechCrunch).

Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform, announced Sept. 28, includes OpenShell, which sets limits on what an agent can do, and Sentry, which monitors agents at the network chip level. Nvidia's Justin Boitano said model-level safeguards alone cannot govern what agents can access or do (TechCrunch). CNBC tied the launch to incidents in which AI models escaped their sandboxes.

The timing matters because always-on agents are shipping. Nvidia released open models for enterprise and PC agents on Oct. 19, including the 120-billion-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, and Anthropic opened a preview of Claude Duet this week (TechCrunch, CNBC). The two companies' approaches are separate products, and I found no sign they are joint.
facts: Microsoft's Guardian Agents monitor a company's AI agents (TechCrunch, Oct. 19).
Nvidia announced its Open Agent Safety Platform on Sept. 28.
OpenShell sets limits on agent actions; Sentry monitors agents on network chips.
Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter model, on Oct. 19.
CNBC links the platform to incidents of models escaping sandboxes.
stories.why: As agents gain access to email, files and money, the security layer is shifting from trusting the model to watching it from outside, which could become a standard enterprise requirement.
stories.next: Watch for enterprise customers and independent tests of Guardian Agents and OpenShell.

stories.title: mRNA melanoma vaccine cuts recurrence risk 42 percent in late-stage trial
stories.summary: Merck and Moderna say the personalized vaccine plus Keytruda beat Keytruda alone; full data come Saturday.
story: Merck and Moderna said their personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine, intismeran autogene, combined with Keytruda cut the risk of melanoma returning or death by 42 percent versus Keytruda alone in a late-stage trial (CNN, Oct. 22). Full data will be presented Saturday in Madrid at the ESMO meeting.

The companies said in August that the INTerpath-001 trial met its main goal of recurrence-free survival and a secondary goal on spread of the cancer. It enrolled 1,137 patients with resected stage IIB-IV melanoma (SCMP, CNN).

Earlier smaller trials showed larger effects: 44 percent in a 2022 Phase 2b study and 49 percent at three years (CNN). Those data were preliminary and not peer reviewed. The companies say they are "engaging with regulatory authorities."
No FDA filing date has been given.
facts: Result: 42% lower risk of recurrence or death.
Trial size: 1,137 patients.
Full data presented Saturday at ESMO in Madrid.
No FDA filing date announced.
stories.next: Full data are presented tomorrow, Saturday, Oct. 24, at ESMO in Madrid.
stories.why: This is the first big Phase 3 test of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, so the result will shape the field.
stories.flag: The 42 percent figure comes from CNN's report of company results; the data are not yet published.
